newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Central African Republic peace deal signed.
newsitem.headline: Central African Republic peace deal signed.

text.p: Central African Republic's embattled president, Ange-Felix Patasse, his political rivals and army mutineers signed a peace deal on Saturday to end an army mutiny and ethnic bloodshed.

Presidents Omar Bongo of Gabon and Idriss Deby of Chad, who launched a mediation process in December with the presidents of Mali and Burkina Faso, attended the signing ceremony in the national assembly in the capital Bangui.

The peace blueprint, agreed after the country's third army mutiny within a year, envisages creation of a government of national unity, amnesties and restoration of constitutional legality within the impoverished nation's democratic transition.

"National reconciliation is a vital commodity, a commodity without end. It's a permanent process to which we must commit ourselves, a flame which must be lit and jealously watched over," chief mediator Amadou Toumani Toure, Mali's widely respected former military leader, told those present.

Bongo said that a 500-strong African peacekeeping force would deploy soon to supervise implementation of the peace deal. It will include soldiers from Burkina Faso, Chad, Gabon, Mali, Senegal and Togo.

"The wished-for arrival of an inter-African mission to watch over the Bangui Accords...will have the mission of facilitating the return of peace and a calming of the tensions in the city of Bangui and in the interior of the nation," Toumani Toure said.
Mutinies in April and May began over pay and conditions but turned into a campaign to oust Patasse, a northern civilian politician who won presidential elections in 1993.
The latest mutiny degenerated into ethnic feuding. The mutineers were from the minority Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba. The overall death toll ran into hundreds.

Mutinous soldiers and mediators signed an accord on Friday formally ending their latest revolt, which began on November 15. Captain Anicet Saulet, leader of the mutineers, was one of those who signed the deal. He made no comment during the ceremony.

The peacekeepers will replace troops from former colonial power France, who have been acting as a buffer between the mutineers and bitter rivals in the presidential guard. Two French soldiers were among those killed in the latest revolt.
The four presidents launched the mediation bid in December at the behest of a Franco-African summit in Burkina Faso.
